retrieval_text: A 34-year-old male presented with nausea, vomiting, and decreased appetite for 10 days. He reported a history of excessive thirst, frequent urination, nighttime urination, and recurrent carpopedal spasms during childhood. He was born at full term via normal vaginal delivery with no complications during the antenatal or neonatal periods. The patient denied any history of limb paralysis or weakness, recurrent urinary tract infections, fractures, hearing issues, or vision loss. There was no family history of renal diseases. Four years ago, his creatinine level was 2 mg%, and he was under the care of a nephrologist. Physical examination showed a moderately built and well-nourished individual with short stature (height: 140 cm) and no obvious deformities or skeletal dysmorphic features.

A six-year-old male from a rural area presented with localized skin changes on the scalp, affecting the right parieto-frontal, left parieto-temporal, and occipital regions. The affected areas included three plaques measuring 8 × 6 cm, 5 × 6 cm, and 6 × 4 cm, respectively, with regular borders. The first two plaques had a red base, hair loss with hairs cut at the same level on the skin, pustules, and honey-colored and blood-stained crusts that fluctuated upon palpation and released purulent discharge. The third plaque showed diffuse hair loss and fine scaling on the surface. Additionally, there was bilateral cervical lymph node enlargement. The patient's mother reported the development of 'pustules' over the past two months, followed by hair loss.

An 11-year-old boy reported difficulty in eating and limited mouth opening for the past year. The patient described experiencing a burning sensation in the buccal mucosa when consuming spicy food during the same period. He had a habit of chewing tobacco and betel nut 15–20 times daily for the past 5 years and often kept the quid in the buccal vestibule. Clinical examination showed a maximum interincisal distance of 13 mm. Intraoral examination identified palpable fibrous bands over the labial and buccal mucosa, along with blanching of the palate, soft palate, and floor of the mouth. Tongue movements were restricted, and the uvula appeared shrunken.

A 21-year-old woman was referred to the department of periodontology at the school of dentistry, Babol University of Medical Sciences for routine dental care. She was born to parents who were not related by blood, both of whom were clinically normal. Her mother was 22 years old and her father was 29 years old at the time of her birth. There were no pregnancy complications, and no other family members exhibited similar conditions. At birth, she presented with craniosynostosis, brachycephaly, and syndactyly of the hands and feet. The patient has mild mental retardation but demonstrates satisfactory social development and bonding skills. She has never had seizures. An extraoral examination showed a brachycephalic skull with midface hypoplasia, a flat forehead, depression of the temporal bones, proptosis, hypertelorism, a short nose with a bulbous tip and septal deviation, and a trapezoidal-shaped mouth. A lateral cephalogram indicated hypoplasia of the maxilla, giving the appearance of a class III skeletal relationship. Syndactylies were observed in the right hand’s third, fourth, and fifth digits and the left hand’s second, third, and fourth digits. Both feet exhibited fusion of all toes. Intraoral evaluation revealed poor oral hygiene with varying degrees of periodontal involvement, an arched swelling (pseudo cleft configuration), class III malocclusion, anterior open bite, posterior cross-bite, supernumerary teeth, ectopic eruption, and creamy white enamel opacities. The tongue appeared excessively large, and the maxillary arch was v-shaped.

A 24-month-old Japanese boy was brought to our hospital for assessment of his short stature. He was born at 38 weeks and 4 days gestation with a submucous cleft palate and micrognathia. His birth weight was 3225 g (+0.53 SD for average Japanese male infants), and his birth length was 45 cm (−1.80 SD). The submucous cleft palate was surgically repaired at 18 months, and tympanostomy tubes were inserted for secretory otitis media. Auditory brainstem response testing was normal. At 22 months, bilateral leukocoria was observed, and phacoemulsification with anterior vitrectomy for bilateral lens opacities was performed at another hospital. He was noted to have Pierre Robin sequence, but the connection to his eye symptoms was not explored. He received speech therapy for speech delay. Upon presentation, his weight was 11.6 kg (−0.33 SD) and his height was 79.1 cm (−2.52 SD). His arm span measured 79 cm, and his sitting height was 48.5 cm (sitting height/height ratio 0.61). Physical examination revealed ocular hypertelorism, prominent eyes due to shallow orbits, a flat midface with a depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nares, micrognathia, low-set ears, and limited bilateral elbow flexion. There was no hypotonia, hyperextensible joints, or joint pain. His family, including his parents and two brothers, were healthy. His parents are not consanguineous. His father's height was 182 cm (+1.93 SD for average Japanese adult men), and his mother's height was 147 cm (−2.09 SD for average Japanese adult women).
A 79-year-old woman experienced a fall while ascending stairs, leading to a chest injury.

A one-year-old female presented with swelling in the right inguinal region. The family history included consanguinity, with the parents being first cousins. Physical examination identified bilateral palpable gonads located in the inguinal area. The external genitalia appeared female, with a slight clitoral enlargement measuring 1.5 cm, and separate vaginal and urethral openings.

An 18-month-old female infant arrived at the emergency department following a brief episode associated with fever. She was born after an uneventful pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks gestation. Her motor and social developmental milestones were achieved within expected timelines, though she exhibited mild expressive speech delay, speaking only five to six words and unable to combine words at 18 months. Family history included a cousin with childhood-onset epilepsy and another cousin with febrile seizures. Upon arrival, the infant displayed lateralized eye gazing, unilateral facial twitching, and unilateral body shaking. She had a fever and upper respiratory symptoms but no signs of serious or central nervous system infection. Postictal examination was reassuring with no focal neurological signs. Extensive infectious workup returned negative results. During her hospital stay, she experienced two additional similar episodes. Due to the recurrence and specific onset characteristics, she was started on levetiracetam for a short-term course.

A 36-year-old male, active smoker with no significant medical history and a family history of cancer in the mother (type unknown), presented with right-sided chest pain for 3 months, worsening over the past 3 weeks. Initially, he visited the emergency department 3 months ago when the pain began and was discharged after pain relief with ibuprofen.

A 48-year-old woman, generally in good health, with occasional smoking habits and no family history of breast cancer, underwent a cosmetic bilateral mastopexy augmentation at age 28. She initially received 380 cc textured-surface implants placed in the sub-glandular plane. A year later, she opted for an implant exchange to 305 cc textured implants in the same plane, along with a re-mastopexy. Three years after that, she received 210 cc Allergan Biocell®-textured round TSM implants, again with a re-mastopexy. Ten years post-surgery, she experienced pain, swelling, and discomfort in her left breast without signs of infection or trauma.

A 3-year-old male child, born to consanguineous parents, presented with global developmental delay, hypotonia, lower limb tremors, and poor feeding. The child had a history of recurrent fever, cold, and cough since the age of 1 year. Over the past 6 months, the parents observed increased irritability. At 2 years old, the child was able to walk with support and speak monosyllables, but subsequently, there was a regression of these learned skills.
A 26-year-old woman reported a gradual decrease in vision over 5 months in her right eye.

This 2-year-old girl is the second daughter of healthy parents with no known consanguinity. There is no family history of neurological or inherited diseases. She was delivered at term via cesarean section following an uneventful pregnancy. Her Apgar score was 9 at 5 minutes. Birth measurements were as follows: weight 3560 grams (50–75%), length 49.5 cm (25–50%), and head circumference 35 cm (50–75%). The neonatal period and early months of life were unremarkable. At approximately 7 months old, cyanosis was noted in her extremities and lips. Psychomotor delay was evident as she did not achieve head control or vocalization milestones. By 1 year of age, she exhibited alternating squints and abnormal head posturing. At 14 months, a neurological examination showed alternating squint, tetraparesis with appendicular spasticity and axial hypotonia, psychomotor delay with poor social eye contact, lack of vocalization, and incomplete head control. The Griffiths Developmental Scale indicated a mental age of 6 months.

A 24-year-old female presented with gingival enlargement. She was born as one of twin females after a full-term, uncomplicated pregnancy. Her parents, aged 32 and 34 at conception, are healthy nonconsanguineous Indian individuals. Clinical examination showed enlargement of the maxillary and mandibular gingiva, including the hard palate, partially or completely covering the crowns of maxillary posterior teeth. Multiple carious teeth were noted, along with prominent labial fullness on extraoral examination. Additional findings included mild mental retardation, hirsutism, large cartilaginous parts of the ears and nose, dysplastic fingernails, aplasia of nails on the last two toes of both feet, and pes cavus deformity.

A 26-year-old right-handed male financial analyst presented with recurrent episodes of rotatory vertigo accompanied by nausea and palpitations. These episodes occurred three to four times daily without any specific time pattern. The initial episode lasted approximately 10 minutes, while subsequent episodes were shorter, lasting 10 to 15 seconds. The onset of these episodes was not associated with changes in head position. The symptoms had persisted for six months and did not respond to physical therapy or Lorazepam. An orthopedist ruled out a cervical origin by noting an almost natural curve of the cervical spine.

A 71-year-old male presented with abdominal distension and no other discomfort. Symptoms of bloating began a month prior and worsened in the week before admission. Two years ago, the patient had physical examinations and liver function tests at a local hospital and received liver protection treatment, but liver function did not improve. Occasionally, the patient experienced yellow urine but no significant physical discomfort. Personal and family history were unremarkable. Upon admission, vital signs were: body temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 68 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 134/74 mmHg, and blood oxygen saturation 99%. Physical examination revealed chronic liver disease, moderately yellowish skin and sclera, but no liver palms or spider angioma. The abdomen was soft, without tenderness or rebound pain. Liver area percussion was negative for pain, and the liver and spleen were not palpable below the ribs. Murphy's sign was negative. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities.

A 15-year-old female presented to an outpatient clinic with a 3-day history of fever, cough, and lethargy. She had no prior medical conditions. On physical examination, she had a fever of 38.3°C, mild tachypnea, good oxygen saturation, and stable hemodynamics. Breath sounds were reduced in the left lung, with crepitation noted at the base.
In March 2017, a 75-year-old male presented with a one-week history of left eye periorbital swelling, forward displacement of the eye, and swelling of the conjunctiva.

The patient is a 9-year-old boy who was first seen at the neurology department at 6 years old. He had been previously admitted to the gastroenterology ward due to ongoing nausea and uncontrollable vomiting, with a notable weight loss of approximately 6 kg over the prior 2 months.

A 28-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented with persistent skin nodules on the trunk and extremities. Symptoms began 4 years ago, accompanied by spiking fever, nausea, and vomiting. These initial symptoms resolved after 6 months but recurred with generalized weakness, joint pain, chest pain, and multiple firm, subcutaneous nodules. The nodules were non-tender, prone to ulceration, and self-resolving.
